description: We are a two-person dev team building a 3D Lunar Landing Site Navigator for The Next Frontier. Using real NASA LRO/LOLA elevation and polar illumination datasets, we combine a Python geospatial pipeline with an interactive Three.js 3D Moon featuring switchable heatmaps for landing suitability, terrain slope, sunlight, and a 29.5-day solar power cycle simulator. Our core duo is set and ready to advance Artemis-era mission planning!
summary:
Project JMC is an interactive 3D Lunar Landing Site Navigator designed to help mission planners, educators, and the public rapidly evaluate landing zones at the Moon’s South Pole. Using real planetary datasets from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO LOLA elevation and polar illumination GeoTIFFs), our Python geospatial pipeline processes 22,500 lunar locations into four switchable 3D heatmap layers in Three.js: Overall Landing Suitability, Average Sunlight, Terrain Slope, and Solar Energy Potential.

To address the extreme lighting and communication constraints of Artemis and CLPS missions, the tool features an interactive 29.5-day lunar cycle timescale simulator showing how solar power shifts across crater rims and permanently shadowed regions, alongside a Site & Direct-to-Earth (DTE) Comms Evaluator. Users can compare candidate Artemis targets or custom coordinates across dates to assess solar elevation angles, sunset countdowns, and Earth line-of-sight windows- accelerating safe mission planning when launch schedules change.
details:
What Project JMC Does & How It Works

Project JMC is an interactive 3D Lunar Landing Site Navigator built to help mission planners, researchers, educators, and the public rapidly evaluate candidate landing zones across the Moon’s South Pole (65°S–90°S).

  1. NASA Geospatial Data Pipeline (Python):
    • Our Python processing pipeline (rasterio, numpy, pyproj) ingests authentic planetary GeoTIFF datasets from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA): South Polar Digital Elevation Models (LDEC_60S_240MPP_ADJ) and average solar illumination maps (AVGVISIB_65S_240M_201608).
    • The script transforms native South Polar Stereographic metre coordinates into lunar latitude/longitude and 3D unit-sphere coordinates across 22,500 polar locations, calculating terrain slope steepness (°), average sunlight percentage (0–100%), daily solar energy potential (kWh/m²/day), and a composite Landing Suitability Score (0–100).
    • Using planar polar UV projection on a custom Three.js polar cap mesh (eliminating traditional pole-pinching distortion), the frontend renders four live, switchable heatmap overlays—Suitability, Sunlight, Terrain, and Solar Energy—paired with a master Heatmap ON/OFF toggle so users can inspect the underlying lunar craters and ridges at any time.
    • Each mode dynamically computes and displays real regional statistics (such as safe flat terrain < 15°, optimal zone counts, and peak solar yield).
    • Exclusively in Solar Energy mode, an interactive timescale slider (Day 0.0 to 29.5 Earth days) with Play/Pause animation simulates how solar azimuth sweeps 360° around the South Pole horizon—demonstrating how Peaks of Eternal Light (like Shackleton Crater’s rim) maintain continuous power while surrounding plains enter the 14-day lunar night and Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) remain dark.
    • A dedicated mission-planning panel lets users select curated Artemis III and CLPS candidate targets (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, Malapert Massif, IM-1 Odysseus, Haworth Crater) or input custom coordinates and landing dates to assess Direct-to-Earth radio line-of-sight (accounting for the Moon's 27.3-day optical libration wobble and Earthset windows), solar elevation angle, and time remaining until sunset.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Rapid Scenario Replanning: Launch delays and hardware constraints frequently force NASA Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) teams to evaluate backup sites and dates quickly. Project JMC replaces fragmented, specialist-only tables with immediate visual and quantitative trade-off comparisons.
  • Accessible STEM Education: Translates complex planetary ephemeris and topographic models into an intuitive browser-based 3D experience that helps students and the public understand why the Lunar South Pole is humanity’s next frontier.

Creativity & Engineering Factors Considered

  • Overcoming Polar Distortion & Terrain Clipping: Standard equirectangular maps stretch severely near -90° latitude, and uneven 3D lunar relief can hide flat overlays. We engineered a planar top-down polar UV cap lifted above maximum lunar elevation peaks so circular craters and ridges render accurately without radial distortion.
  • Real Lunar Physics Constraints: We incorporated low polar solar elevation angles (~1.5°–10°), permanent shadow ice traps (< 5% illumination), safe lander slope thresholds (< 15°), and optical libration (±7.9°) affecting Earth horizon visibility.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Languages: Python 3, JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5, CSS3
  • Geospatial & Scientific Libraries: rasterio, numpy, pyproj
  • 3D Visualisation & Frontend: Three.js (WebGL), HTML5 CanvasTexture, Vite
  • Collaboration & Development Tools: Git / GitHub, Visual Studio Code, macOS say TTS (for demo narration), and AI coding assistance (OpenAI Codex / LLM guidance for boilerplate scaffolding and debugging).
